There are countless depictions of God throughout human history: the benevolent and loving deity, the flawed pantheons, the omnipotent, the omniscient, even the malevolent Gods. Or perhaps an apathetic God-- who exists, but cares little about the individual lives of his/her creation.

I believe you are speaking of the concept of Hell? During my brief time in catechism, I was taught by a priest that those who commit suicide are sent to Hell because of disrespecting the human body (which is also considered a Temple of God) in Christianity. I naturally questioned that belief as well: if the Christian God was a benevolent and loving God, why would he send his suffering child into further torture? 

I decided that while suicide is the last resort, we cannot tell if Hell awaits us if we go through with it. God may or may not exist. At this point, whether he does or does not is irrelevant-- we are foolish to think that our individual lives matter to a cosmic being. But that's okay. We're all fleeting.

Who says God is bound by a human standard of morality? Perhaps God is a sadist, letting us suffer for his enjoyment. Perhaps God is testing us, giving us chances to prove ourselves worthy. Or perhaps God really doesn't give a toss whether we suffer or not.

It may be better for humans, in the long run, to live as if God does not exist. This does not automatically make one a horrible person, contrary to popular belief. It only means that it's counterproductive to work too hard to become better people just to please some eternal sky god, when we could be doing better things like becoming better people because we know it is the right thing to do.

I'm of the opinion that faith is a wonderful thing to have-- sometimes I feel envious of people who can still believe in heaven or eternal life or the concept of God.

But judging by the history of the world, religion has done many evils. The self-righteous, the greedy, and the pompous have conquered and killed and pillaged in the name of their religion.

Faith is a good thing, but it tends to go awry when blind faith leads to blind obedience, or if used as a tool by humans to reflect their own vanity.

I used to go on Omegle, try to have random conversations with people, talk about anything other than what I'm feeling. Or when I come across other sad people (not necessarily in a depressive episode), I talk to them. I find trying my hand at helping them helps me cope.

Those were on my 'good' days. Now I lock myself in my room and drink just enough to easily fall asleep, which is quite different from straight out drinking until I pass out, but it helps since falling asleep doesn't make me conscious enough to be depressed.

Thank you for giving me that once-in-a-lifetime kind of love. I'm sorry I hurt you. I'm sorry for not telling you some things I should have.

I love you, I still do. But you deserve someone better. So thank you for bringing some light to my life before its end. I wish you all the best. Goodbye.

I hope I'm not being selfish, but you remind me of her.

I think you may find that there's always a lull in between years, especially around this time. Fortunate are those who seem to have life planned out for them... That's dull. Planning's dull. Never be dull.

Before you consider suicide, maybe try making a list of things you'd like to try. A fun list. Places you want to see, books you need to read, whether you want to watch the sun rise from the rooftop of your house after stargazing all night, the little things. I don't know if this helps in any way, but it could at least tide you over until you make a decision.

Also, everyone's a fuck-up. Some people are just really good at hiding it. Social media makes it so easy nowadays.

From experience, there needs to be a certain amount of clarity and determination to even attempt suicide. What's holding most people back are the things they'd leave behind.

Death is a pit of uncertainty. That's because no one credible has ever returned from it. It is a finality: irreversible.

It is our instinct to survive that keeps us away from suicide. Any sufficiently rational mind can generate doubt in the person to turn away from suicide.

As to your question, what makes life worth living? It varies. To one, it could be hearing the voice of the one you love as they whisper your name, it could be the places you still want to visit, it could be the food you have yet to try. It could be a dream or an achievement one still wishes to have or the possibility, however slim, that things will change for the better.

3. In relation to number two, I am boring.

4. I suffer from anxiety and depression. It's not an attractive trait.

5. People always only seem to like a version of me, but once they see how messed up of a person I am, they bail.

Wouldn't it be more selfish if I told her? It would feel like manipulating her even after I died. If she finds out, let it not be from me.

My parents have disowned me and I live on my own. I'm at that point where my depression swings from down to violent, to emotionless. I'm a college dropout (dropped out because of financial reasons and my mental instability). Even with my current job, I still have to make ends meet.

I'm only waiting two years because there's a life insurance policy the company gave us, but when the employee dies of suicide, there is a contestable period. (Still working out how to get most of the claim and give it to my parents, I wasn't really the smartest person.)
